en: Commentary on the Verses on the Regulations of the Eight Consciousnesses: Verse on the Five Consciousnesses: "Nature-objects, direct perception, and the three natures; (it is precisely because the true nature is not understood that so many deluded natures arise). The three—eye, ear, and body—dwell in two stages. *Note: "Nature-objects" refers to objects as they truly are, prior to conceptual construction. "Direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) means cognition free from conceptualization (*vikalpa*). "The three natures" refers to the fact that these five consciousnesses can correspond to all three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—depending on the mental factors associated with them. The phrase in parentheses indicates that the failure to realize the true nature leads to the proliferation of deluded states. These five consciousnesses reside in the first two *bhūmis*: the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna of the Form Realm.*
"Who can obtain even a small portion of these five consciousnesses? (The eleven universal, particular, and wholesome [mental factors]—indeed, many such deluded thoughts.

"The two intermediate [unwholesome] and the eight great [afflictions], along with greed, anger, and ignorance—deluded thoughts reach their ultimate limit here. "The five consciousnesses rely together upon the pure material sense organs (which are fundamentally and originally pure).

The nine, eight, seven, and six are naturally adjacent to one another (yet alas, they are disturbed by them). Combining three and separating two to contemplate the mundane world (one must instead look directly within the five sense organs to see through the functioning of those organs). The fool..."
It is difficult to distinguish consciousness from the sense faculties—who, indeed, can understand this? To perceive emptiness through transformed appearances relies solely on subsequent attainment;

even if one can prevent consciousness from being disturbed by conditions, this only saves half the work. Even within the state of fruition, the ultimate truth is not yet fully articulated. When perfect luminosity first arises, it becomes the outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
With the three types of emanation bodies, the wheel of suffering is brought to rest—returning the five consciousnesses to their wondrous function to deliver sentient beings.

The meaning of Master Xuanzang’s verse on the five consciousnesses is as follows: When the five consciousnesses descend upon the gates of the six sense organs and illuminate their objects, at that moment, neither inference (*anumāna*) nor testimony (*āgama*) has yet operated; it is merely a presentative cognition (*pratyakṣa*) arising momentarily through discrimination.
However, this is not the realm of one who has attained awakening, for they immediately follow along with conditions and delusions. Thus, as soon as a thought stirs, [it is already lost].
One must enter into the eighty thousand nets of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). These include the universal mental factors, the object-specific ones, the twenty secondary afflictions, and so forth;
it does not suffice merely to observe them through the sixth, seventh, or eighth consciousnesses as they pass by.

When one knows the moment of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), countless thoughts arise and perish within the mind—whom can escape this? As the former Buddhas said: "The moment you raise your mind, worldly afflictions appear first."
It is so. At this time, one uses medicine to treat the illness; how does one apply the hand? One also examines within the five consciousnesses:
why do three of them combine, and why do two of them separate? Furthermore, consciousness resides within the faculties, and the faculties reside within consciousness.
Ultimately, toward what place does consciousness arise? If you can cast a single eye upon this very point and distinguish it clearly, this is precisely it.
This is also the news of awakening. If one merely transforms thoughts to contemplate emptiness, one remains bound by the gate of contemplation;

even if one possesses insight, it is still merely subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) and not fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). One will thus fail to reach the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
It is simply a matter of awakening once and for all, so that at the very moment the five consciousnesses first arise, one awakens to the initial manifestation of perfect luminosity.
How could it merely give rise to errors regarding the two stages? I know the principle of the three types of manifested bodies;
one can directly take responsibility for them right now with full capacity.
The objective realm of direct perception (pratyakṣa) pervades all three natures.
These three natures are precisely the realm of non-awakening. The nature of goodness settles into white karma;
the nature of evil settles into black karma. Thus, one is bound by cause and effect and cannot attain sovereignty.
That which is neither good nor evil appears to be still and silent, yet it actually falls into the confusion of ignorance—the malady of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). This is the first [point].

First, regarding those who are pitiable: they are those who hold views of stubborn emptiness or nihilism, or who fall into the three types of non-conceptual retribution. They repeatedly receive these states of indeterminate consciousness (*avyākṛta*).
Therefore, it is only when pure wisdom is wondrously perfect and its essence is inherently empty and quiescent that one reaches the ultimate state.

If one were merely empty and quiescent in a singular sense, that would simply be the state of indeterminate consciousness. Although these three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are pervasive within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), direct perception is in fact dependent upon these natures.
Regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*): why is it said that the objective realm is the "nature-realm" (*xingjing*)?

It is because when one seeks to contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one realizes that all things are created solely by the mind. Thus, the Pure Radiance Bodhisattva shifted the realms and stages to appear at the tip of his finger;
the moonlight appeared within a room of clear water; Ucchuṣma’s entire body became fire; and Vairocanaraśmipratimaṇḍitavigraha’s whole body became wind. Is this not the objective realm?

Is this the realm of intrinsic nature? Yet, because one has never thoroughly awakened to and broken through that realm, when encountering objects, good and evil suddenly arise, and one is entirely turned by those objects;
thus, one remains silent in the face of objects, unaware of where they truly fall.
People within the three realms do not know what these three realms are; they have not yet contemplated escape from them.
They are like turtles inside a jar who, to the very end, do not know what the jar is. Even if they were to engage in dull deliberation, they would possess no wisdom at all.

They merely fall into the state of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If one can, like Lingyun, pierce through the peach blossoms, or like Dongshan, awaken to the reflection in the flowing water, how could one ever be dominated by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) such that it would pervade the three natures?
The three faculties of eye, ear, and body reside in two stages;
these five consciousnesses conjoin with the five objects. Who can escape this within the realm of desire?

Within it lies the stage of the mixed dwellings of the five destinies, which is the first stage. Among its inhabitants, there are those who sleep, those who eat and drink, and those who engage in sexual desire.
The five consciousnesses are all complete [in the desire realm]. Only in the first dhyāna of the form realm—known as the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion—is this the case;

it is the second stage. The devas and humans therein are frequently in a state of meditative concentration. Because they are weary of this coarse material food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra), although they possess a nose, they do not actually cling to odors;
although they possess a tongue, they do not actually cling to tastes. Thus, two of the five consciousnesses—the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses—are diminished.

However, the two consciousnesses of the nose and tongue actually exist; advancing from there, they are still present within the Form Realm, specifically in its three stages known as the Three Dhyānas.
Advancing further, they are likewise present within the Formless Realm, specifically in its four stages known as the Four Emptinesses.
The above comprises the nine stages (*bhūmi*). In the first stage, the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) of devas and humans are still turbid.

From the second stage up to the ninth, the five consciousnesses gradually become clear, yet they have not finally reached the untainted nature of consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna-svabhāva*). Nevertheless, these devas and humans can become Buddhas.
It is like making a pickle out of vegetables; by no means should we, base and inferior ordinary fools, instead look down upon Bodhisattvas who sport in the celestial palaces.
[The eleven wholesome mental factors] are the universal, the object-specific, and the wholesome.

The universal [mental factors] are fivefold. Through countless kalpas, they have become deluded into the seeds of the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), like fish submerged in a deep pool that stir up waves which surge forth of their own accord;
this is called *manasikāra* (attention). It draws the mind toward its objects; this is called *sparśa* (contact).
It contains and does not relinquish [the object]; this is called *vedanā* (feeling). It causes the shadowy image of the external object to appear vividly before one; this is called... [perception].
*Saṃjñā* (perception) is the subtle, uninterrupted process of searching with effort; this is what is called *cetanā* (volition).
This is the most subtle point within the single thought-moment that creates both good and evil.

Generally, from the moment one clings to an object, as soon as a thought moves and attention is directed, there is no object—whether it be the object of contact, sensation, perception, or volition—that is not reached. This clinging to an object pervades [all experience].

Because they operate across all eight consciousnesses, all nine stages, and at all times, they are called "universal" (sarvatraga). There are five object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-pratiniyata-ālambana*). These are:

first, *chanda* (desire), which is the aspiration to act toward an object that one finds pleasing. Second, *adhimokṣa* (resolute confidence), which is the determination regarding an object that it can be accomplished, such that one cannot help but proceed.
Third, *smṛti* (mindfulness), which causes the mind to clearly retain and remember an object that is to be accomplished. [The text continues: "It is called..."
To focus the mind one-pointedly upon the object of observation is called *samādhi*; this is different from the *samādhi* of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
To have a clear and unerring understanding of the object of engagement is called *prajñā*; this is different from the *prajñā* of transcendent wisdom (*paññā*).
Generally, when one clings to a single thought-moment—this very thought, refusing to let it go—is what constitutes desire (*rāga*).
They are resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). These constitute the nesting place of the nature of consciousness;
because they differ from those that take objects as their focal points (*ālambana*), they are called "distinctive objects" (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*). Regarding the eleven wholesome [mental factors]:

what was previously termed "universal" and "distinctive object" refers to the mind that initiates action but has not yet performed it. Upon reaching the eleven wholesome factors, however, the action is fully completed. First.
First is faith; second is shame; third is remorse; fourth is non-attachment; fifth is non-hatred; sixth is non-delusion;
seventh is diligence; eighth is serenity; ninth is heedfulness; tenth is equanimity; and eleventh is non-harming.
Although the five consciousnesses are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*) and appear as if unconditioned, their karmic nature is fully matured; thus, they are merely incidental.
At the moment a single thought arises, if it is unmoving, it abides on the side of the wholesome; if it is fixedly moving, it abides on the side of the unwholesome.
If it moves toward the wholesome, then among the eleven types of wholesome karma, those who possess the five consciousnesses cannot avoid them.

To cause one to realize the nature of Consciousness-Only by including this [point], one comes to know the proportions of wholesome karma attained; only then will one not depart from the wholesome, yet remain unattached to the wholesome. Thus...
To perform even a single virtuous deed is not merely the accumulation of merit for rebirth as a Brahmā; it is simply the turning of the compassionate vows of Samantabhadra.
[The middle two are the eight great [afflictions]: greed, anger, and delusion.]
This is precisely the karma of committing evil deeds. There are twenty-six such evil karmas in total. There are six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*):
namely, greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong view. As for the branches that grow from these roots, there are ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), namely:
anger, resentment, vexation, concealment, deceit, guile, arrogance, harmfulness, envy, and stinginess; as well as shamelessness and lack of dread.

These two are the medium universal mental factors (*upakleśa*). Lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, lethargy, restlessness, loss of right mindfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and distraction—these eight are the great universal mental factors.
They are termed "small," "medium," and "great" because they perform a single function.

When they function as a single karma, they are called "small. For example, when shame (*hrī*) is necessarily accompanied by dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), it constitutes a single karma that simultaneously induces two karmas;
this is called "medium. When performing a single karma yet being able to pervade all defiled minds, it is called "great.
Thus, the karmas of the small-universals are heavy, yet they are regarded as small; the karmas of the great-universals are light, yet they are regarded as large. This is because...
Based on the root, the branches and leaves immediately arise; this is what consciousness values, as it is observed within the realm of mental deliberation.

Now, while the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) follow [the afflictions] only slightly, we speak here only of the two medium and eight great [afflictions], because among those associated with the five consciousnesses, these alone are direct [associates].
This refers to the fact that among the twenty-six types of afflictions, there are the two medium and eight great ones, along with greed (*lobha*).

Anger and ignorance—these together constitute thirteen kinds. If one can awaken to and clarify the nature of consciousness, then there is the "skillful lust" of Vāsuki, the "skillful anger" of insatiability, the "skillful envy" of Devadatta, up to the "skillful greed" of the three carts and the "skillful killing" of Nanquan.
Whether Buddha or Mara, good or evil—it is the realm of the inconceivable.
Yes. The five consciousnesses share a common support in the pure material sense organs (*viśuddha-rūpa-indriya*).

These have "dust-like" sense organs (*paricaya-indriya*), which are composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Within these four great elements, the ultimate sense organs (*paramārtha-indriya*) are hidden. And...
It is difficult for the foolish to perceive, as if they were blind. Yet the nature of seeing remains; though the ears are blocked, the nature of hearing remains.

This is called the *paramārtha-indriya* (the faculty of ultimate reality). Therefore, the treatise states that the body is fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning, which is what is meant by "ultimate nirvāṇa.
When wisdom transforms into consciousness, and consciousness becomes stagnant, it forms the faculties (*indriya*). Thus, one is bound and obstructed by ignorance.

The aggregates of form coalesce to form the sense organs, and within them, the essence of ignorance and consciousness takes up residence. Ordinary beings of the lower realms certainly cannot be separated from their physical, ephemeral organs;
even the intermediate state body possesses a form, and those in the Heaven of No-Thought ultimately possess a lifespan.
Extending this reasoning to the devas of the formless realm down to those in the four stages of emptiness, they still possess material substance.
This is because while one can empty the karma of consciousness, one cannot empty the nature of consciousness; thus, their physical faculties remain characterized by either heaviness or pliancy.
There is that which is neither existent nor non-existent and capable of transformation; yet it can ultimately never transcend the realm of the nine stages (*navabhūmi*).

This is because it carries the consciousness (*vijñāna*) of ignorance, taking the aggregate of consciousness as its faculty. Only for the Greatly Awakened Bodhisattvas are their two bodies—the retributive (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya*)—also pure material faculties (*rūpendriya*).
However, since these three bodies are of one essence (*trikāya-ekamūrti*), their features are difficult to discern. Therefore, universally...
The eye does not see the body of Samantabhadra; Mañjuśrī did not behold the face of Kāśyapa. Thus, where could the bell-shaker of Universal Transformation (Puhua) gallop?
Where in heaven did the sandals of Bodhidharma rest? Is it not like the moon piercing the bottom of a pond, where the water is boundless?
This is what is meant by the five consciousnesses relying together upon the pure material sense-faculties (*rūpa-indriya*). Such is the view of the ignorant.
To recognize only that the eye is like a cluster of grapes and the ear is like a fresh curled leaf is truly laughable.
When the nine conditions and the seven or eight [consciousnesses] are favorably adjacent,

and the five consciousnesses rely upon the same pure faculties while being conditioned by defilements, one then perceives the sequential order of the eight consciousnesses, each having its own [distinct nature].
Regarding the objective conditions (*ālambana*), the verse states: "Visual consciousness arises from nine conditions; auditory consciousness from only eight;

olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses from seven; and the final three from five, three, and four respectively. If the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is added, one is increased for each starting from the beginning.

Thus, visual consciousness possesses nine conditions: first, space (*ākāśa*), which refers to the empty space that provides an opening; second, light, namely the sun, moon, and lamps; third, [the object].

1. The faculty (*indriya*): this refers to the primary faculty. 2. The four objects (*viṣaya*): these refer to that which is seen. 3. The fifth is attention (*manaskāra*): this refers to attention among the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

4. The sixth is the support for discrimination (*vikalpa-niśraya*): this is the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). 5. The seventh is the support for defilement and purity (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-niśraya*):

this is the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*). 6. The eighth is the fundamental support (*mūla-niśraya*): this is the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). 7. The ninth is the condition of seeds (*bīja-pratyaya*): this refers to the eye...
Consciousness is the seed that directly produces [perception]. People know only that the eye can see;
they do not know that the act of seeing is induced by various conditions, and that it actually arises from the false seeing and discrimination of the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses.
Therefore, when one consciousness is deluded, all consciousnesses are utterly deluded; when one faculty awakens, all faculties awaken simultaneously—this is precisely that meaning.
When Kāśyapa caught sight of the lotus, and Xue Qin pierced the ancient cypress, was their causal origination not non-arising?
As for the ear-consciousness, it follows only eight [conditions], excluding the condition of light. For the nose, tongue, and body, there are twenty-one [conditions] in total. All are...

This excludes the two conditions of space and light. Regarding the subsequent [passages] "five, three, four, three," this refers to the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses having five conditions, three conditions, and four conditions respectively.
The sixth consciousness possesses five conditions: first, the root-condition (*indriya-pratyaya*), which is the seventh manas-consciousness;

second, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), which refers to the eighteen *dhātus*; third, the attention-condition (*manaskāra-pratyaya*), which is among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).
This refers to the mental application (*manasikāra*). Fourth is the fundamental condition (*mūla-pratyaya*), which is the eighth storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

Fifth is the seed-condition (*bīja-pratyaya*), which refers to the seeds directly produced by the fundamental consciousness. The seventh consciousness possesses three conditions; the first is the seed-condition.

This refers to the seeds directly produced by the fundamental consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Second is the condition of mental attention (*manasikāra*), which is the mental attention among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).

Third is the condition of the sense organ and its object; that is, the eighth storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) serves as the root for the seven consciousnesses, and through this, they perceive the objects of the five sensory realms.
The eight consciousnesses possess four conditions: the first is the condition of the sense organ, which is the *manas* (seventh consciousness).

First is the causal condition of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Second is the causal condition of objective conditions (*viṣaya-pratyaya*), which refers to the seeds, the root-body (*mūla-śarīra*), and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).

Third is the causal condition of attention (*manasikāra-pratyaya*), which is one among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*). Fourth is the causal condition of seeds (*bīja-pratyaya*), which refers to the direct productive seeds of the eighth consciousness.

If one adds the causal condition of equal and immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) to each of these from the beginning, it means that the preceding moment has already ceased and the succeeding moment...
It arises again; this is called the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). When these nine conditions are augmented by this one condition, these nine conditions become ten conditions.
Other conditions follow this same principle. In general, the nature of this consciousness is like the blood vessels of a person, circulating throughout the limbs and body;

with every breath, all the channels are set in motion. Thus it is said: "Universally manifesting, it encompasses all lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; when withdrawn, it gathers them back in."
Within a single mote of dust, how can one bear to allow such a supreme treasure to be submerged amidst the conditions of nature?
"The union of three and the separation of two" refers to the mundane world as the object;
"three" and "two" refer to the faculties. One speaks of separation and union by means of the faculties illuminating the objects, as in the case of the nose, tongue, and body.

One apprehends objects through contact, for it is only through contact that they are known. As for the two faculties of eye and ear, they apprehend objects while separated from their respective organs, because contact would otherwise destroy the organ.
Is it that the application of the organ differs—one preferring contact and the other preferring separation—or is it that the application of consciousness differs?
Ultimately, does one perceive worldly objects through contact, or ultimately through separation?
When observing the dust of the world, within the midst of union and separation, one can realize the affairs of one's own house;
how could it be that one uses them daily yet remains unaware? Furthermore, Nalakalīpa saw without eyes, and Śāriputra heard without ears.
The Ganges does not smell odors with its nose; Brahmā does not know tastes with his tongue; the spirit of space has no body to perceive touch.

Are these [sensations] separated from or conjoined with the sense organs (*indriya*)? Are they the sense organs themselves, or are they consciousness (*vijñāna*)? I have great expectations for the wise one regarding this.

It is difficult for the ignorant to distinguish between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the sense-faculties (*indriya*). The faculties are material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), specifically the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness. Consciousness is a mental phenomenon (*citta-dharma*), specifically the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect) of the eighth consciousness;
thus, matter and mind are distinct. Furthermore, the faculty can illuminate the object, while consciousness can cognize the object; this is the distinction between the faculty and consciousness.
Their functions differ. The five external objects serve as the remote *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eight consciousnesses;

the five internal faculties serve as the intimate *nimitta-bhāga* of the eight consciousnesses. Therefore, the eighth consciousness and the five faculties are both of an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature.

Consequently, while the five consciousnesses possess *anusmaraṇa-vikalpa* (recollection-based discrimination), they lack *abhinirūpaṇa-vikalpa* (conceptualization-based discrimination). Thus, they are constantly intermingled and difficult [to distinguish].

[The author] distinguishes [the following]: the natures of these faculties (*indriya*) and consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are not the same. The Śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle who adhere to the Dharma of the Ignorant know only that the faculties and consciousnesses arise in mutual dependence;
they do not know that both the faculties and the consciousnesses each possess seeds and manifesting states (*samudācāra*).

While it may be said that the faculty serves as the condition for the arising of consciousness, it cannot be said that it gives rise to the consciousness itself, for consciousness possesses its own seeds capable of producing it.

For this reason. I say: apart from the sense organ (indriya), there is nothing by which consciousness (vijñāna) can be manifested; apart from consciousness, there is nothing by which the sense organ can be supported.
The organ and consciousness are like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other; they lack individual self-nature (svabhāva) and thus seem as if they cannot be separated.

Because of the organ, there are appearances (nimitta); because of appearances, there is seeing (darśana). This consciousness arises from the organ. Because of consciousness, there is the organ; because of the organ, there is seeing. This organ...
It arises from consciousness. Furthermore, it cannot be understood unless one distinguishes it.
Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* discerns the nature of consciousness as being neither born from another, nor born from itself, nor born from causes and conditions, nor born without cause.
By ultimately tracing this place of arising to its very root and bottom, one is said to be able to distinguish between consciousness and the sense faculties.

In the contemplation of the emptiness of the transformed aspects (*pariṇāma-nimitta*), it is only through the subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) that one clearly understands the outflowing nature (*sāsrava*) of the five consciousnesses. Upon reaching this stage where the evolving consciousnesses are transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*), one is able to empty the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses that constitute their own immediate manifestations;
this too is a portion of the subsequent attainment wisdom. This is because, if one were to rely on a dull emptiness (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*), [the transformation would not occur].
If one is entirely devoid of wisdom, one is biased toward emptiness and possesses but little insight. Thus, the ancients said: "The twenty gates of emptiness are all unattached;
the single nature of the Tathāgata’s essence is inherently identical. When one is thus able to transform appearances, the eye does not become attached to form.

Since the twenty afflictions and other coarse delusions have already been eliminated, this is not fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); rather, there is subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
"Subsequently" is said in contrast to the fundamental. Within this subsequently attained wisdom, there is the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

In reality, there exists a gate of cultivation and realization; yet, because the views regarding phenomena (*dharmadṛṣṭi*) have not been exhausted, even within the fruit [of Buddhahood], true fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*)—which relies on the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) and is able to directly perceive *tathatā*—is still not fully articulated.
Subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), however, relies on the material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and possesses partial [perception].

It is distinct. Within the state of Buddhahood, there still remains a single speck of dust [of separation]. People know only Master Tai’s commentary, which—based on the words of Master Sthiramati—asserts that subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) exists within the first five consciousnesses;
that because it has already become untainted (*anāsrava*) during the causal stage, it transforms its appearance to take the suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.

Master Dharmapāla refutes this, stating that the two divisions of the seeing and the perceived aspects still belong to the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and only upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood [are they transcended].
Regarding the stages: only the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is able to directly perceive *tathatā* (suchness). How could it possibly transform into an image to perceive suchness?
People stubbornly cling to the distinction between cause and fruit, taking this to be the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), yet they are unable to realize the Path itself.

Little do they realize that "when the fruit ripens, the stalk remains suspended" is spoken from the perspective of ultimate realization. If awakening is not thoroughgoing, how can it be considered ultimate? Furthermore—

How could this be considered awakening? Awakening consists precisely in seeing through the nature of consciousness (*vijñaptimātratā*) and thoroughly penetrating the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As for the pervasive and specific mental factors, as well as the coarse and subtle afflictions and karma—all these are defiled by non-awakening (*abodha*).

Once one attains awakening, it is like a single lamp that can shatter a thousand years of darkness in a room; thus, the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, and the fruition penetrates back to the cause.
The source is precisely the realization of truth within the fruit. How could it be that one waits for awakening with the mind? How could it be that one abandons awakening to seek realization?

How could it be that one awaits the welcoming descent of a transformation Buddha, or that the physical form changes through retribution, such that only by sitting in meditation and entering samādhi can one enter the stage of fruition and attain supernatural powers?
Therefore, realization is subsumed within awakening; true awakening is itself true realization. It need not be otherwise.
I maintain that others have attained the stage of realization; I merely fear that there are no people in this world who have awakened.

When the initial arousal of perfect clarity achieves the state of non-outflow (*anāsrava*), the sixth and seventh consciousnesses transform during the causal stage, while the fifth and eighth consciousnesses reach perfection upon the fruition stage. Now, the five consciousnesses arise from within the eighth consciousness.
The seeds are stored within; fundamentally, there is no worldly entanglement—this is what is meant by having "thick roots" from former lives.
Thus, they are entrusted to the gates of the five faculties. When the visual consciousness perceives forms, it is like Kāśyapa’s seeing through the plucking of the flower;

when the faculty of hearing hears sounds, it is like Avalokiteśvara’s awakening to the dissolution of the locus of perception. In both cases, one remains unattached. Through cultivation, realization, and diligent refinement, this is simply...

If one suddenly attains perfect clarity by returning to the point of initial awakening, that itself constitutes the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). It is identical to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom;
once this is realized, everything is realized, and there remains no further trace of outflows (*āsrava*).

The three classes of transformation bodies that cease the wheel of suffering consist of three types of emanations: for those of great capacity, a large body is manifested; for those of middling capacity, a medium body is manifested; and for those of small capacity, a small body is manifested.
These transformation bodies are subsumed within the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the reward body is subsumed within the dharma body (*dharmakāya*). One is able to perceive them only by oneself.

One's own nature is the complete embodiment of all bodies. Let us inquire: as for the locus of the seeing of the five consciousnesses—is it the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the three natures (*svabhāva*)?
Is it the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the object-specific factors (*viśeṣabhūmika*), or those possessed of various afflictions (*kleśa*)? Ultimately, what is this?

It cannot be identified as something fixed within the categories of the Dharma-numbers of the *lakṣaṇa* school (the Abhidharma). Nor can it be identified as the "seeing-portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses.
This is how it arises. One must not regard it as a manifestation of ignorance accumulated over countless kalpas. Have you not heard?
The various illusory minds of sentient beings all arise within the Tathāgata’s wondrous, perfect *bodhi* mind.

If one awakens to and shatters this [delusion] right here and now, then when greed and anger arise, nirvāṇa manifests; when deluded thoughts are produced, the Buddha-way is accomplished. It is no other than this.
Free from the outflows of the shell, he manifests immeasurable bodies to deliver sentient beings and bring rest to the cycle of rebirth.

○ Regarding the verse on the six consciousnesses, the three natures, the three means of valid cognition, and the three objects: (If a person can understand that the great earth of the mind is not even an inch of soil), the turning of the wheel of the three realms can easily be known (ultimately...).

Objects are created from the mind. The fifty-one mental factors associated with it are all contained therein. Whether they are wholesome or unwholesome, they are assigned accordingly at each moment, each following its own kind.

The natures, realms, and sensations constantly shift and change (moment by moment, without ceasing). The faculties and their concomitants, such as faith and so forth, are all interconnected (driven by a single mechanism).
Movement of body and utterance of speech are preeminent (these are the leaders). The power of karma that draws and fills exerts its pull (thereby bringing about retribution).

One initiates the initial mind on the Stage of Joy (capable of destroying afflictions). Yet innate tendencies still manifest as entanglements and latent seeds (the attachment to dharmas remains). From the Far-Reaching Stage onward, they are purely non-existent.
The outflows [of the mind] blossom forth in brilliance. Observing with perfect clarity, it illuminates the great chiliocosm;
there is no dharma that is not realized. Master Xuanzang said: "The general principle of the six consciousnesses does not exceed a single thought-moment.

The clear and knowing mind (*manas*) appears to lack power, as it cannot couple with its objects as truly as the five sensory consciousnesses do. Nevertheless, the sixth consciousness possesses the five consciousnesses. This is certain.

The solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is of five types: first, the solitary mental consciousness in the state of meditative absorption; second, the solitary mental consciousness in the state of distraction; third, the solitary mental consciousness in dreams;

fourth, the clear and distinct mental consciousness; and fifth, the distracted mental consciousness. Furthermore, consciousness possesses five conditions: first, the condition of the sense organ (*indriya*);

second, the condition of the object (*viṣaya*); third, the condition of attention (*manasikāra*); fourth, the fundamental condition; and fifth, the seed condition (*bīja*). These five conditions apply to the five [sensory] consciousnesses as well. The fundamental...
Regarding the three measures, the three natures, and the three objects, there is no karma that is not received. The fifty-one mental factors are thus comprehensively subsumed.
That which is seen by the five external sense organs all arrives at the head of the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
While what is seen has not yet ceased its discrimination, that which is grasped by the seventh and concealed by the eighth [consciousnesses] likewise turns toward [it].
The meaning of the sixth [consciousness] is that when discrimination returns to the head, it is as if something like a pulley were turning incessantly within the chest;
how much more so when it continues without interruption—how could one possibly attain purity in a single kṣaṇa?

Thus, by means of the three natures, one creates the three types of sensation: good sensations are the retribution of good fruits, and evil sensations are the retribution of evil fruits; those that are neither good nor...

Evil, neutral, and indeterminate [actions] receive their retribution; these constitute the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) and the completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*), both of which have the six [sense bases] as their root.

With the exception of the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the cessation attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*), sleep, and fainting, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) may temporarily cease to function, yet its roots ultimately remain.
One must first attain the nature of a noble one (*ārya-gotra*), fully realize the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), and reach the first stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

By means of this, one possesses pure ethical discipline and reaches the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*); possesses superior meditative concentration and reaches the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*);

gives rise to sublime wisdom and reaches the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*); is difficult for worldly things to overcome and reaches the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*); abides in the knowledge of dependent origination and reaches the Ground of Manifestation (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*);
transcends effort and surpasses the two vehicles, reaching the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*). Thus, the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) of the first ground—

Reaching this point, all [delusions] are completely shattered. This refers to one who employs the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for discernment; by reversing this, it becomes the wondrous observing wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

Yet, when seeking the karmic retribution of the three feelings (*vedanā*), they are found to be utterly unobtainable. Is this not indeed the practitioner’s realm of great enjoyment? Ultimately, what constitutes the perfect clarity of observation?
Is it not the gate of contemplation as a remedial countermeasure? This, however, remains an attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Is it not perhaps to ensure that not a single thought arises? This is still the mental faculty (*manas*) speculating and forming various interpretations.
To search for the mental faculty is like this: "The boat lies across the wild ferry, holding autumn’s azure; the oars enter the reeds, reflecting snow-bright clarity."
The three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the three means of valid cognition (*tripramāṇa*) apply to all three objects; these three natures and three means of valid cognition are easy to understand.

However, if one carefully analyzes the three objects, when an object is defined by its nature (*svabhāva*), it is like the pure water of merit or the palaces that accompany the body—are these not created by nature? There are two types of objects of nature (*svabhāvaviṣaya*): first, the sense organ...

Dust (dharma) is indeed the color-form of the fixed fruit, produced by the deluded karma shared by the eight consciousnesses. The two wisdoms, because they fundamentally take suchness as their object, also have this as their sphere;
that is to say, the Land of Common Abode for Mundane and Holy Beings. Regarding the "bordered substantial" object, there are two aspects: the substance and the subject.
Within the substance of the external object, it is like tea being water; this refers to the category of that which serves as the primary substance. As for "bordering,"...
To say that this does not exist is to see it as something brought over from that [external object]; this is the "externally defiled" (wài-rǎn) type.

Once brought onto the body, the entire person engages in mental construction, like a single *qīngfú* (copper coin) for which hundreds or thousands [of others] rush about. Whatever objects the ordinary body clings to are all termed "brought-to-the-substance" (*dàizhì*).
Thus, the "brought-to-the-substance" type encompasses both the "sentimental" (*qíng*) and the "fundamental" (*běn*), serving as that by which sentient beings are stuck and obstructed.

It is as if it were "resembling a substantial object" (*sādṛśya-savipaya*). That is to say, these six consciousnesses can take the objects of the external environment and make each one clearly manifest within the mind.
This is a "semblance-object" (*pratibimba-viṣaya*) appearing before [the consciousness], arising from the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the sixth consciousness.

This is called the "seeing-part resembling a substantial object," and it is not the true [object]. Therefore, it is said that when the mind takes form as its object, it resembles a substantial object; the intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) is one [of these].
"Born within the head. Regarding "born within the head": this means that the substance of the six consciousnesses is fundamentally pure and devoid of any objective entity.
Now, when analyzed in terms of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) arising through false perception, it appears as if there is a single object with substantiality born within.

The second is "the true with the associated substance" (*zhēn dàizhì*). This refers to the seven consciousnesses. Because the seven consciousnesses grasp the seeing-part (*jiànfēn*) of the eighth consciousness as a self, they proceed outward through each of the five sense faculties.
For example, when greed for form arises, it brings forth the objective substance (*jìngzhì*) of the form that is the object of greed to confront the sixth consciousness;
thus, it is not a mere semblance. Therefore, it is said: "With the mind taking the mind as its object, it is truly associated with the substance."

Substance. The intermediate aspect arises at both ends. As for "arising at both ends," this does not mean that two single moments arise, nor does it mean that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses manifest at both ends. It means that every thought-moment is attached to form;
thus, what is sincere within naturally manifests outwardly. "Arising at one end" would still mean having a beginning but no end; now, however, there is...
The head has a tail. The sutra states that there is no transmission of consciousness that does not function to its utmost; therefore, it is said that "it arises at both ends.

There are two types of solitary-reflection objects (*ekacchāyā-viṣaya*): first, the solitary reflection without a real substrate, such as when the sixth consciousness perceives flowers in the sky or the horns of a rabbit.

And [this includes] the objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed from the past, future, and so forth. Second, there are those with a basis (*sadravya*) and those that are mere shadows (*pratibimba*).
This refers to the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) taking the seeds and manifestations of the five sense organs as its objects; these all rely upon a basis to give rise to their objective images.

However, they cannot directly experience [the object], but merely arise from the same seed as the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), and are thus also called "mere shadows. Regarding the statement that the sixth consciousness pervades the three types of objects: this refers to what is seen by the five consciousnesses.

When the sixth consciousness does not engage in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it apprehends the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of its object; this is the "objective realm" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).

When it takes as its object a mind or mental factor (*citta-caitta*), it is the "realm with substance" (*sadravya-viṣaya*). When it takes as its object a phenomenon lacking substantial reality, it is the "solitary image realm" (*kevala-pratibimba-viṣaya*).

The object is the "object-condition" (*ālambana*), and consciousness is the "subject-condition" (*ālambaka*); each possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The objective realm, which does not depend on names or conventional expressions, has its activity (*kriyā*) as its nature. The subject-condition...
Excluding the manas-vijñāna, the remaining six [consciousnesses] all take their own mind and mental factors as their substance.

Regarding the object of solitary reflection (pratibimba), it takes the provisional aspect (nimitta-bhāga) transformed by the sixth consciousness’s seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) as its substance; the perceiving subject takes its own mind and mental factors as its substance.

Regarding the object with a core (sanimitta), it takes the provisional aspect transformed in the intermediate state as its substance; the perceiving subject consists solely of the six [consciousnesses].

The seven consciousnesses and their associated mental factors take the mind and its concomitants as their substance. Thus, the verse says: "Substantial objects do not follow the mind; Solitary images arise only from the aspect (*darśana-bhāga*);

Objects with a core-penumbra (*sanimitta*) pertain to both the subjective and objective. By clarifying these three types of objects, one may hope that the sensory dust will dissipate and awareness become pure.

Not only must one not be attached to the objects themselves, but one must also not be attached to the core-substance, nor even to the images. Only then is it truly the "mind-only" of the subtle dust motes and oceans of lands.
Mirror: throughout the realm, white jade lotuses bloom.
When the wheel of the three realms turns, it is easy to see and know;
yet as the divisions are not pure, they are stained into the two natures of good and evil, which bring about the experience of suffering and pleasure in the future.
Second, as for retribution: even if one is deluded, ignorant, and lacks knowledge, one still cannot escape this jar of the triple world.
The cause of the triple world is fixed: through delusive ignorance there is empty space; based on space, worlds are established; through the solidification of false thoughts, lands are formed;
and from the emergence of cognitive awareness, sentient beings are born. If direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is already empty, then inference (*anumāna*) cannot fail to be non-arising. Thus:
The exhaustion of the mind within the three realms is called *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, one should know that the three realms cannot bind me;
it is I who create the three realms—what can they do? Those who are well-bound by wholesome karma cannot attain autonomy; those who are constrained by unwholesome karma cannot attain autonomy.
Even if one reaches the Peak of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, when their lifespan is exhausted, they are still [bound].
Kegon! Why not crush through empty space, severing the limits of the past and future, to emerge beyond the heavens?
The fifty-one mental factors associated with consciousness are fundamentally empty and quiescent;
they originally have no location. There is nothing like the nature of awakening that is not limpid. [This is realized] through the three measures and the three natures.

Within [the manas], there appear the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the five object-specific factors (*viśeṣabhūmika*), the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala*), the six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*). These constitute the fifty-one mental concomitants (*caitta*).
Other consciousnesses cannot fully possess them all; it is only when the great consciousness and the manas are individually analyzed that such a multitude arises.
The thought of discrimination is called the "distinctive object. This discrimination necessarily arises from all objects in all nine stages;
that which is thought of at all times is called the "universal. When discrimination is wholesome, it cannot be separated from the eleven types of wholesome factors.
When discrimination is unwholesome, it likewise cannot be separated from the twenty-six [unwholesome factors].
These various unwholesome dharmas—whether they manifest as good while being evil, or as evil while being good;
whether they arise from delusion and ignorance, or from clarity and awareness—are all produced from within the four states of non-concentration.
They are collectively initiated within the three natures and the three modes of cognition, and are collectively contained within a single moment of non-awakening. Therefore:

Seeing a palace maiden holding one’s feet, one immediately knows the transgression of illicit intimacy; hearing the sound of bracelets touching the ear, one immediately knows the breaking of precepts.
From these causes, one thereby knows the resulting effects; from the root, one thereby knows the encompassing branches.

Therefore, while the faculty of the mind has not yet attained awakening, how can one lightly stir a thought? As the former Buddhas said: "By all means, do not trust your own mind; your mind is not [to be relied upon]."
This is credible; it is for this reason. The six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) are greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong view.
These six are the roots of the two kinds of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*). Among those that sever the life-force of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*), these alone are most severe.
The four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*) are regret, sleep, vitarka, and vicāra. Regarding "indeterminate," it is like a person who has committed an evil deed.

To reform and turn toward the good: when one sleeps, the mind becomes extremely obscure; this is neither good nor evil, and is termed "indeterminate. Vitarka (applied thought) is necessarily the intention to perform good;
it involves mental deliberation. When coarse, it is called vitarka; when subtle, it is called vicāra (sustained thought). It is like praising a Bodhisattva:
only after initial vitarka followed by vicāra does one obtain sublime words. It is also like a litigant who likewise [proceeds] by...

Only upon entering the stages of vitarka (initial inquiry) and vicāra (sustained investigation) can calculation be successfully accomplished. These two factors may be wholesome or unwholesome; they are indeed indeterminate.
Whether wholesome or unwholesome, they are assigned accordingly according to the circumstances.

Once the seeds of karma are fully present, they will spontaneously manifest when encountering conditions within the mind. I have often observed that those with auspicious minds possess a virtuous disposition.
Thus, his speech is excellent, his vision is excellent, and all aspects are excellent. Conversely, for an evil person, all three are unwholesome.
These various wholesome and unwholesome dharmas each correspond to the individual with whom they are associated.
If one is a wise master, one will accept neither the Goddess of Merit nor the Woman of Darkness.

The three types of feeling—of nature (*dhātu*), of sphere (*āyatana*), and of experience (*vedanā*)—are constantly shifting. Although there are three [categories], in reality there are five: namely, painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*), pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*), sorrowful feeling (*daurmanasya vedanā*), joyful feeling (*saumanasya vedanā*), and neutral feeling (*upekṣā vedanā*).

That which afflicts or gratifies the body is called physical pain or pleasure; that which afflicts or gratifies the mind is called mental sorrow or joy. Thus, sorrow and joy, as well as pain and pleasure, [are distinguished].
When neither [pain nor pleasure] is active, it is called neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Now, within the sixth consciousness, either through black karma one constantly revolves in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and experiences painful sensations, or through white karma one constantly revolves in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpya-dhātu*) and experiences pleasant sensations.
Indeed, having a body is inherently suffering; even for devas who enjoy pleasures, the five signs of decline eventually manifest—how can this truly be happiness?
To have a mind is inherently sorrowful; even for the Brahmakāyika gods whose merit is exhausted, afflictions suddenly arise of their own accord—how can this truly be joy?
Moreover, the rapid alternation between rising and falling is like a mustard seed within the vastness of space. All [are impermanent].
The places where I have cast off my life since being liberated from the cycle of bones exceed Mount Sumeru in height; such is the number of times the wheel has turned.
One must contemplate the arising and ceasing of thoughts without departing from perfect stillness (*parinirvāṇa*). Both the mundane and the supramundane are entirely *nirvāṇa*;
thus, one may approximate the truth without falling into the fallacy of the moving shore while the boat remains still.
"Roots and their attendants" refers to the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). "Faith" refers to the faculty of faith among the eleven mental factors.

"And so forth" refers to the universal (*sarvatraga*), object-specific (*viniyata*), and indeterminate (*aniyata*) mental factors. Regarding "connected in their general characteristics": although the body...

Although the differences in the retributions one receives inevitably lead to changes in form and appearance, this *karmic consciousness* among the fifty-one mental factors remains unchanged to this day.
Whether it be wholesome, the wholesome dharmas still manifest; whether it be unwholesome, the unwholesome dharmas still manifest.
This is what is meant by "habit becomes natural"; one falls into the net of Māra without even realizing or knowing it.

Regarding the statement that movement of the body and the utterance of speech constitute the primary [manifest] discourse, it is said: "By externally manifesting body and speech, one expresses what is thought within the mind. It is like a fish submerged in a deep pool, which causes waves to surge forth.

This consciousness possesses three types of volition (*cetanā*): first, the volition of deliberation (*paryeṣaka-cetanā*); second, the volition of determination (*niścaya-cetanā*); and third, the volition of instigation (*abhisamskāra-cetanā*).
It is superior thought (*vijñapti*). It is most excellent because it is absent in other consciousnesses. Yet, this arising of speech does not occur apart from the tongue;
nor can the tongue itself produce the nature of sound. Ultimately, from where does it arise?

Therefore, by means of consciousness one may recognize the nature of consciousness, and by means of sound one may awaken to the Way. It is like the moon in a clear pool: one knows it only when one reaches out to grasp it.
Regarding "projecting" (*ākṣepa*) and "fulfilling" (*paripūraṇa*): that which can project is the projecting karma; that which can fulfill is the fulfilling karma.

There are cases where a single karma projects a single fruit, and there are cases where a single karma projects multiple fruits. Regarding retribution (*vipāka*), there are two types of fruits: collective and individual. As for the collective:
Thus, while one generally attains a human body within this realm, there are distinctions such as the differences in status between the noble and the lowly among humans.
Now, by means of the six consciousnesses and the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*) manifest;

yet, regardless of whether one is an inferior ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) submerged by conditions, a practitioner (*śaikṣa*) still falls under the sway of fetters and karma, or even a Bodhisattva who remains separated from the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*), this is truly what is called "fixed karma" (*niyata-karman*).
It is impossible to escape. Unless one attains great enlightenment, one must employ *prajñā* (wisdom) to dissolve [delusions] amidst favorable and adverse circumstances;
then, affliction and bodhi, as well as karmic bondage and liberation, will be seen as no two different things.
Upon attaining the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), which is the first resolve, the innate afflictions still manifest as active entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The "active entanglements" refer to the functioning of the eyes, while the "latent tendencies" refer to the seeds.

Because the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the six consciousnesses is conflated with the afflictions into a single mass, even though one has reached the Stage of Joy, the innate grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the innate grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) still persist.

It lies latent within the sixth mental faculty, like a eyeball that has not yet left its socket. When one reaches the emptiness of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the innate tendencies (*sahaja*) still remain.
How can those of today, whose entire bodies are permeated by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), yet claim to have realized the Way, be anything other than deluded Chan practitioners?
After the Ground of Far-Reaching Travel (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*), one is purely free from outflows (*anāsrava*). With observation perfected and luminous, one illuminates the great chiliocosm.

The innate dual grasping at self and dharmas (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) is that which is clung to by the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*). Since the seventh consciousness lacks the power to sever delusions on its own, it must also rely upon the sixth consciousness;

through the contemplation of the twofold emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), all attachments are shattered. Thus, by awakening to and clarifying the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), one passes through and leaves behind [all obstructions].
The stages of the Stainless, Luminous, Radiant Wisdom, Difficult to Conquer, and Manifest reach this stage of Far-Going (*dūramgamā*).

When what has been realized is no longer shallow, the innate outflows (*sāsrava*) are forever suppressed and do not arise; the associated mental factors (*caitta*) are transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), capable of preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings and possessing great eloquence (*pratibhāna*). This manifests clearly in every head and shines forth in every object. It is thus here.
Alas! People today fall into a state of neutral indifference (*avyākṛta*), where their afflictions (*kleśa*) momentarily subside; they then claim that their mental faculty (*manas*) is pure.
How could they know that the thieving mind has not yet died? To tether a horse, to suppress a rat, or to practice a daze in stagnant water—what is there to say of such dead Zen?

The verse on the seventh consciousness states: It possesses a "substantial" nature and is obscured; it pervades both the mental factors (*caitta*) and their bases (*āśraya*). Following conditions, it clings to a self, its scope being erroneous.

The eight universal factors and the specific object-factors are associated with wisdom. Greed, delusion, the view of self, and pride accompany it. These four afflictions are particularly tenacious as it constantly and thoroughly deliberates.
The notion of a self (the self-grasping that arises simultaneously with its fruit) follows me; sentient beings are perpetually deluded day and night—how could they not fall into birth and death?

The four afflictions and eight major [secondary] afflictions arise together (the nature of karma does not cease). The six evolving consciousnesses are called the basis of defilement and purity (they are linked to the six sense organs).

The state of equality at the stage of "Supreme Joy" and the initial resolve (is it not a nature-borne, obscured state?)—I constantly crush non-effortful practice (it is not constant and investigative deliberation). When the Tathāgata manifests, others receive [his teaching].
[It is] used (for transmission, being excellent in both respects). It is the karma-clad state of Bodhisattvas on the tenth stage (where the Dharma-cloud universally covers).
Master Xuanzang’s general meaning is that these seven consciousnesses are called *manas*, because their essential nature and characteristic consist in cogitation (*manana*).
It is also called "transmission," because its function is movement; it is also called "sustenance," because its adherence to the self is firm;
and it is also called the "basis of defilement and purity," because it relies upon the six consciousnesses.

Thus, its objects are not shadows of intrinsic nature, but rather possess substantiality and are obscured. Its activities and functions always serve as the foundation for the delusion of sentient beings.

Its mode of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is neither inference nor direct perception; it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) according to conditions. It pervades both the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), and this is considered its reckoning as non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Therefore, while there are twenty-six afflictions (*kleśa*) in total, this consciousness has as its nature the defilement of present activity;
thus, it is associated with the eight [secondary] afflictions. Lack of faith, laziness, and heedlessness are conjoined with the obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) state.
It is characterized by an unserviceable state [of mind] and lethargy; it is frequently accompanied by agitation and restlessness; and it is often accompanied by wandering and distraction.
It is capable of giving rise to afflictions, and manifests as the loss of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension.

Furthermore, it is associated with the five universal mental factors—attention, contact, feeling, perception, and volition—and is also associated with the discernment (prajñā) among the five object-specific mental factors. This is because...
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is precisely the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). Because this consciousness spontaneously engages with its object without any expectation, it is distinguished from desire (*chanda*).

Because this consciousness takes a specifically determined thing as its object, it is distinguished from resolve (*adhimokṣa*). Because this consciousness constantly takes as its object a present, presently experienced thing and lacks any act of recollection, it is distinguished from mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Because this consciousness spontaneously takes distinct objects moment by moment and is not focused on a single point, [it is distinguished from concentration].
To distinguish them: self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), and self-love (*ātma-sneha*) are called the four afflictions (*kleśa*).

The ten derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*), such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth, which are associated with these [four], are coarse and agitated in their manifestation; since this consciousness is subtle and refined, it does not coexist with them. Among the intermediate derivatives, there are two:

It is exclusively unwholesome. Because this [consciousness] is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is not associated with those [wholesome factors]. Since the eleven wholesome factors are pure (*śubha*), they do not coexist with this consciousness, which is defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
This consciousness possesses three conditions: it possesses the condition of the seed, the condition of mental attention (*manasikāra*), and the conditions of the sense organ and the object.
Taking the "substantial core" as its object, having "cognition" as its nature, and taking "self-grasping" as its root, there then exists—
Do the mental states not fall into confusion day and night? Furthermore, because there is the *ālayavijñāna*, there is the *manas*.

Because the *manas* exists, it serves as the support for the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). Because the six evolving consciousnesses exist, the five manifest consciousnesses are able to function based upon them.
This seventh [consciousness] universally takes the faculties, objects, and conditions as its basis; it evolves depending on them and perceives those very objects. What is this?
The six modes of transformation are called the basis for defilement and purity. Although the seventh consciousness possesses self-clinging, it is in reality devoid of a self-nature;
thus, it can function as either the sixth or the fifth, and it may follow either defilement or purity. Only those who have attained awakening can skillfully employ it.

If the six consciousnesses are able to awaken to and enter the dual-emptiness contemplation that eliminates both self and dharmas, this constitutes the transformation into the untainted (*anāsrava*) at the initial mind of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
At this time, one realizes the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), such that among all actions and deeds, not a single dharma falls into the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
This includes those states characterized by substantiality, the obscured (*nivṛta*), and those that grasp at a self according to conditions—all of these are completely dissolved and explained away.
Regarding the wisdom of equality, how could one not be able to expound the Great Dharma to benefit all sentient beings?

As for "that which possesses substance and is obscured" (dai-shi yu-fu), it penetrates both the phenomenal aspect and the fundamental essence; why does that which possesses substance and is obscured penetrate both the phenomenal and the fundamental? Observe, for instance, the body as it clings to sensory objects: every thought-moment remains therein.
In this regard, it is not that the mind is obscured; rather, the communication of emotion is rooted in the fundamental nature.

Thus, regardless of whether ordinary beings in this realm are constrained by physical form, the two heavens dwelling on earth engage in sexual union; in Yāma, they embrace; in Tuṣita, they hold hands;

in Nirmāṇarati, they exchange smiles; and in Paranirmita-vaśavartin, they communicate by gazing at one another—all of these involve a substrate of matter as the basis for the communication of emotion.

Furthermore, the fundamental basis for the attachment of these seven consciousnesses is precisely that which arises carrying the essential substance of the root of craving of the eighth consciousness.

Consequently, its obscuration of the true nature is already exceedingly profound. One explanation states that when the mind takes the mind as its object, it truly carries the "substance" (the essence);
from this, the intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) arises at both ends: one is the [aspect] belonging to the seventh consciousness...
It transforms. First, it is that which is subsumed within the eight consciousnesses; hence it is said that "it arises at both ends.

Following conditions, it grasps at a self and takes its own measure to be other than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*); it is also that which arises within the constant and thorough investigation (*santīraṇa*). Nevertheless, it is that which is induced by the five sense-faculties and their respective consciousnesses.
The seventh consciousness functions spontaneously for these. It transmits the creations of the inner six [consciousnesses] and the eighth consciousness;
thus, that which clings to a self according to conditions is, by measure, most frequent.
It is like a person calling out one's own name and one immediately responding. At the moment of response, the mouth, ears, and body all move together—is this not the transmitting consciousness?
When called, I respond. Is this not the grasping of a self? Since I respond immediately upon being called, am I not turning toward and depending upon that [self]?

Yet at this time, one does not engage in conceptual calculations based on inference; is this not non-inferential cognition (*anumāna*)? Because I respond due to the call, there is no "I" acting as a sovereign master;
is this not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

The eight universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and the object-specific factor of wisdom (*prajñā*)—namely, greed (*rāga*), delusion (*moha*), the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and pride (*māna*)—are associated with wisdom.
Wisdom belongs to the category of object-specific factors (*viśeṣa-bhūmika*). Greed and delusion are two of the root afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*).
Self-delusion, the view of self, pride, and self-love are called the four secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), or alternatively, the four afflictions. Based on this, this consciousness governs only...
It maintains and transmits [objects], and is categorized as non-cognizant (*avyākṛta*) and not being a valid means of cognition (*apramāṇa*). For what reason is it fully endowed with all afflictions?

It is because this consciousness possesses constant and thorough deliberation and is capable of performing mental attention (*manasikāra*); it can also cling to objects and serve as both universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) [mental factors].
Whether pure dharmas or unwholesome dharmas, there are none that it does not produce together. This is unlike the five consciousnesses, which each belong to [their own specific] category.
A single faculty cannot function simultaneously with others; it is not like the six consciousnesses, which can merely perform empty conceptualization but cannot directly experience objects.
Thus, this faculty of thought is extremely subtle and its power is exceedingly great.
Constantly and critically deliberating on the accompaniment of the notion of self, sentient beings are perpetually and deeply deluded day and night.
The first five consciousnesses are not constant because they perceive objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) which is intermittent; they are not critical because they do not grasp at a self.

The sixth consciousness is both critical and constant, yet it is also subject to interruption. Only the seventh consciousness is both constant and critically examines [its objects]. As for the eighth consciousness—
This perception is divided into a self, which then correlates with and follows along [with other mental states].

For example, during seated meditation, when the five consciousnesses manifest objects, they do not arise abruptly without cause; yet, if within stillness one suddenly moves toward a single objective condition, this is a shadow manifested by what is stored within the eighth consciousness.
This is then grasped by the seventh consciousness and constantly conceptualized, rather than being subject to constant, thorough examination.

Indeed, that which is conceptualized is taken as distraction and agitation; does it not thereby entangle the six sense faculties? Therefore, the six [faculties] repeatedly rely upon this as their master.
All of this occurs because the mark of self (*ātman*) is firmly established. One must constantly and carefully examine this; such examination is itself the process of deliberation (*manas*).
This deliberation is itself the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*), and this grasping at a self is the delusion of the seventh consciousness.
To perceive [objects] is the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Yet, the deluded do not awaken; they instead cling to the conscious spirit (*vijñāna-ātman*) as their own self-nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, they are truly immersed in daily life, lacking the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) for even a single moment.
The four delusions and eight major afflictions arise in conjunction; the six evolving consciousnesses are called the basis of defilement and purity.
These seven consciousnesses are fully endowed with the four delusions and eight major afflictions; they are truly defiled consciousnesses. Nevertheless, delusion and awakening depend upon the person.
If one attains wondrous awakening in a single thought-moment, causing the *ālayavijñāna* to become clear and pure, then the deliberation of the seven consciousnesses—
As for the "grasper": it is pure in both states and remains unstained. Together with the six consciousnesses, it relies upon this purity and remains unstained.
This seventh consciousness ultimately possesses no self-nature; it is left to the enlightened one to effect its transformation.
The nature of equality at the stage of initial resolve in the Ground of Supreme Joy—I constantly subdue the effortless activity [of the afflictions].
Each of the seven consciousnesses arises simultaneously with the grasping of self;

they grasp at a self while being distinct from non-self, and they grasp at phenomena while being separate from the forgetting of phenomena—this is inequality. Now, from the first ground, the mind is generated.
At that time, without relying on deliberation and without clinging to vitarka and vicāra, one simply uses the mental faculty (manas) to awaken to and shatter the self.
Directly forgetting all effort, one completely penetrates the attachment to dharmas. Thus, emptiness merges with emptiness, and water pours into water;
when one seeks for any of the universal or specific mental factors (caitta), they are utterly unfindable. Is this not the wisdom of equality?
The Tathāgata manifests as the Enjoyment Body for others, serving as the objective capacity for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
Since my seven consciousnesses are set in motion by this, and my entire body is thus the Wisdom of Equality, it does not merely benefit myself.
Furthermore, it can benefit others; it enables those who see and hear it to both partake in the faculties and nature of a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages.

Those of superior capacity are likewise recipients of the teachings I bestow. It is like the Buddha manifesting a body one hundred *zhang* tall, sitting upon a lotus flower with a hundred petals, and preaching the Perfection of Giving (*dānapāramitā*) for those on the First Stage;
or manifesting a body one thousand *zhang* tall, sitting upon a lotus flower with a thousand petals.
This refers to the teaching of the *Śīla-pāramitā* for those on the second bhūmi.

Yet, by condensing the great into the small and transforming the many into the one, even a single minute particle (*paramāṇu*) of the present moment becomes a jewel-king (*ratnarāja*), turning the Great Dharma Wheel.
At that time and in every place, all are simultaneously the receptive vessels (*bhājana*) for the tenth bhūmi.

The eight consciousnesses, in their nature, are exclusively non-obscured; five are universal mental factors (how excellent this memory!). Their realms and stages arise according to the power of karma (and yet they remain indeterminate).

The followers of the Two Vehicles fail to understand them due to deluded attachments (failing to awaken to the eight consciousnesses); because of this, they are able to engage in disputes with the Master (only those with the eye of wisdom can know). Vast indeed are the Three Piṭakas!

Inexhaustible is the flow of birth and death; the profound depths have seven waves stirred by the wind of objective conditions (the inexhaustible causes and conditions). Perfumed and holding seeds, the root-body and the vessel-world (the world and its life depend on others);

departing later and arriving first, acting as the presiding lord—this is birth and death. Before the Immovable Ground, one merely abandons the storehouse consciousness; only through a single awakening is it fully understood.

After the Vajra Path, the ripening consciousness is empty (the realm after awakening). The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the stainless [wisdom] arise simultaneously (returning to that which is stainless). Universal...
"Shining throughout the dust-motes and lands of the ten directions" (upon realizing that there is only consciousness).
Master Xuanzang’s general meaning was this: the nature of the eight consciousnesses is able to contain and store the shadows of past and future conditions that have ceased;
how could it be something that can be covered over or obscured? Furthermore, its fundamental nature is neither good nor evil, and it belongs to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Helplessly possessing the four conditions, it is able to act as the universal mental attention (*manasikāra*).

Thus, that which is a deluded vision of a single thought-moment is accumulated and becomes the seed of the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Therefore, the nature of the three realms and nine stages is fundamentally non-existent;

yet, by means of this consciousness, objects are created, and in turn, those objects dazzle the consciousness. Consciousness and objects depend upon one another, forming a bond so firm it cannot be broken—all of this is due to this very consciousness.

It is merely brought about by the power of karma. Thus, because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not believe in the existence of the eight consciousnesses, it leads to disputes among the masters of the Mahāyāna treatises.
