How could they know that regarding the essence and function of the eight consciousnesses: first, there is the consciousness that acts as the "capable storehouse" (*nengcang shi*), because it can contain and store the seeds of good and evil;
second, there is the consciousness that serves as the "object stored" (*suocang shi*), because it receives the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of manifest activity.

First, it is that which is perfumed; second, it is the consciousness that serves as the storehouse; and third, it is the consciousness that can grasp the seven consciousnesses as "self" and can grasp the four great elements as indestructible.
Possessing these three stores, it governs the conditions of the sense faculties and their objects. Thus, the eight consciousnesses are the deep pool and the seven consciousnesses are the waves.
When the wind of objects blows upon the waves, such that the fifth, sixth, and seventh consciousnesses become turbulent winds and waves, how could the pool ever remain clear and still?
Ah! The winds of objects are the deluded perceptions of sentient beings. If deluded perception does not arise, then the waves will subside and the abyss will become still;
what fault would there be in the eight consciousnesses? It is only when the winds of objects blow upon the waves that the abyss becomes ripples.

These ripples are inexhaustible. Thus, the eight consciousnesses receive perfuming and maintain seeds, thereby bringing about the realms of the sense organs and their environments within the cycle of birth and death.
As for the retribution of past and future lives, who other than the eight consciousnesses could be its agent?

For one who has attained great awakening, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), their tainted habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have been thoroughly seen through and penetrated. From the moment of intentional application (*manasikāra*), these are completely dissolved and exhausted;
thus, every thought-moment enters the Vajra Samādhi. This is the relinquishing of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) and the emptiness of the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*).
Because there is no consciousness of form within the eye, and no eye within consciousness of form, both eye and consciousness are utterly pure;

this is called the meaning of non-arising. By means of this, the ear, nose, body, and mind each function in concert, unified as one—a great, perfectly round, stainless mirror that reflects both before and behind. Thus, the eye can truly see, and the ear can truly hear.

The governance of the nose allows for smelling; the governance of the tongue allows for tasting; the governance of the body allows for touching; the governance of the mind-organ (*manas*) allows for discernment;
the governance of the *manas* consciousness allows for application; and the governance of the *ālaya* consciousness allows for grasping.

This is because they constitute the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). When seeing, what is ever the eye? When hearing, what is ever the ear? When smelling, what is ever...?
The nose—how could it ever be the tongue? Contact—how could it ever be the body? Discernment—how could it ever be the mind (*manas*)? Functioning—how could it ever be the *manas*?
Appropriation—how could it ever be the *ālayavijñāna*? Because it is the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
Thus, seeing is neither seeing nor not seeing; hearing is neither hearing nor not hearing; smelling is neither smelling... [and so forth].
It is not that one does not smell; it is tasting, yet neither tasting nor non-tasting. It is touching, yet neither touching nor non-touching.
It is discerning, yet neither discerning nor non-discerning. It is employing, yet neither employing nor non-employing.
It is grasping, yet neither grasping nor non-grasping. To cut through both ends simultaneously is the wisdom of equality. It is thus.
The three wisdoms are merged and transformed, utterly devoid of mental traces. When gathered back, they are simply one stainless, perfect mirror.
This is the primary principle for those who realize the four wisdoms within the single mind and comprehend all phenomena within the eight consciousnesses.
Its nature is exclusively non-obscured and universally pervasive across the five [mental factors]. Regarding its realm and stage, it arises according to the power of other karmic forces.
Fundamentally, the nature of this consciousness is truly neither good nor evil; it is nothing more than the indeterminate and non-obscured (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*).

Therefore, its objects are not "substantial" (*sadravya*) but are "shadowy images" (*pratibimba-mātra*), and it is dissociated from all phenomena, whether defiled or pure. Alas, as for its capacity...
Through mental attention (*manasikāra*), the mind is drawn toward its objects; thus, among the five universal mental factors (*pañca-sarvatraga*), there is no impurity that is not concealed.

Therefore, this consciousness serves as the sovereign lord of the total retribution and the substance of the destinies and births. Furthermore, the three realms and nine stages all arise solely through the power of other karmic forces.
It is like dry soil, which cannot hold itself together into a single mass, but by means of water, glue, and the like, that dry [soil] is bound together.

Earth becomes a neutral phenomenon (*avyākṛta-dharma*) only when it can form vessels and aggregates; it is through the power of wholesome and unwholesome karma that the realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*) are established.
Because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand this cause and remain deluded in their attachments, they are able to give rise to disputes with the Master of Treatises.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "The ādāna-vijñāna is profound and subtle;

containing all seeds like a torrential stream, I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, fearing they would conceptualize and grasp it as a self. Ādāna, in the language of Tang (Chinese), means "grasping" (*zhíchí*).
Because the eighth consciousness can maintain the seeds without destruction, it is also called "grasping. [This is] the firm [view] of the Hīnayāna.

They cling to the six consciousnesses and do not believe that the eight consciousnesses function as causes and conditions. Furthermore, they do not believe that the eight consciousnesses function as the basis for saṃsāra and its cessation;
they hold them to be merely the support and sustenance [of the mental factors]. For this reason, the Mahāyāna masters have distinguished [the eight consciousnesses] by means of ten verses of proof.
The ten verses of proof state: "The mind that maintains the seeds is the ripening consciousness; it is the consciousness of rebirth, existence, and sensation;
it is the condition for birth and death, the support, and nutriment; and it pertains to the cessation-attainment and the defiled and pure minds.

Since beginningless time, because this consciousness serves as the support for all phenomena, it also serves as the support for manifest phenomena. This proves that there is a mind that maintains the seeds. Furthermore, it says: "There is the wholesome..."
The mind of evil, perfumed through successive kalpas, is called the *vipāka-citta* (maturation consciousness). It is that which brings about the fruition of wholesome and unwholesome karma;
for if this consciousness did not exist, that maturation-consciousness could not exist. This explains the maturation-consciousness.

When sentient beings transmigrate through the five destinies and four modes of birth, if this consciousness did not exist, the substantial basis (*ātmabhāva*) of those destinies and births could not exist. [This is because] the first five...
That which is induced by the karma of consciousness does not lead to rebirth in all destinies, because it is entirely absent within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Although that which is induced by the karma of mental consciousness leads to rebirth in all destinies, it is not constantly present; it exists only as the resultant mind (*vipākacitta*) and its associated mental factors (*caitasika*).
This is because it is the primary cause for the continuity of birth. Furthermore, a sutra states: "The physical body endowed with sense faculties is that which is appropriated (*upātta*).

If this consciousness did not exist, such appropriation would be impossible. This appropriating mind is exclusively the *vipāka* (maturation) mind; the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) do not possess this characteristic.
This explains "appropriation" (*vedanā*). A sutra also states: "Vitality (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these three are mutually dependent."

It maintains [the body] so that it may continue to abide. Because the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) lack the function of constant maintenance—much like sound or wind—and only the maturation consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) possesses this function of constant maintenance, it is established as that which sustains life, warmth, and consciousness. This explains "consciousness. As the Sūtra says:
"When sentient beings pass away, they necessarily abide in a distracted state of mind, not in a mindless meditative absorption. Furthermore, at the time of birth and death, the body and mind...
In a state of profound stupor, such as during sleep without dreaming or at the moment of extreme fainting, the clear and distinct mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) certainly does not manifest.

Furthermore, the modes of activity and objects of the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) cannot possibly be known; this is the "mind with scattered existence," which is called the "mind of birth and death.
One should know that there exists a separate class of subtle mental consciousness whose modes of activity and objects are both indistinguishable and indestructible.

This is precisely the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Furthermore, at the time of death, due to wholesome or unwholesome karma, the sensations of cold gradually arise from the lower or upper parts of the body respectively.
If this consciousness did not exist, these phenomena would not occur, because the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are incapable of appropriating the body.

This proves that the mind of the eighth consciousness constitutes birth and death. Moreover, it is said that consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and name-and-form conditions consciousness.
These two dharmas depend upon one another in mutual succession, like bundles of reeds, evolving simultaneously.

Those evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñānas*) lack the power to constantly sustain name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), yet they always serve as conditions for name-and-form. This "condition" refers to this eighth consciousness;
this explains the nature of the condition. As the Sūtra states: "All sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment. [The same applies to] the evolving consciousnesses.
It is incapable of sustaining the body and life; rather, it is its ripened consciousness (*vijñāna*) that constitutes the nature of superior nutriment. This explains the basis of nutriment.

The Sūtra states that for one abiding in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the activities of body, speech, and mind are all ceased without exception, yet vitality (*āyuṣka*) and warmth (*uṣman*) still remain, the sense faculties (*indriya*) do not perish, and consciousness does not depart from the body. By this principle, it is certain that for one abiding in the attainment of cessation...
This continuous flow of the eight consciousnesses can be understood by analogy in states such as the non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

This explains the mind in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). The Sūtra states: "Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is purified, sentient beings are purified.
If this consciousness did not exist, the minds of defilement and purification would not be possible. That is to say, the phenomena of defilement and purification depend upon the mind.
Birth depends upon the mind for its abiding. This consciousness is the source of both purity and defilement. The general meaning is this:

if this single thought-moment is not awakened to, it becomes the seed of either defilement or purity. These seeds—whether defiled or pure—are distinct from one another, yet they continue incessantly from moment to moment;
this is termed "vipāka" (ripening). This ripening necessarily leads to rebirth within the realms and stages of existence.

Even though there is grasping (*upādāna*), one cannot be separated from the characteristics of the body. That which causes the certainty of sensation (*vedanā*) is the union of earth, water, fire, and wind, which forms the breath of respiration;
this is called the cause of maintaining life-force (*āyuṣka*) and warmth (*uṣman*). It is for this reason that there are the characteristics of birth and death.
When the conditions for entering the womb are determined, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arises, just as one perceives the sun's light and [the visual consciousness] is produced.
Heavenly One, one sees that human beings are born from the fire of lust. Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is conditioned by consciousness (vijñāna), and consciousness is conditioned by name-and-form;

these two are never separate. When it comes to the reception of the sense-faculties (indriya), they can never be separated from nutriment (āhāra). Thus, those who achieve the faculties from beginning to end all have the eight consciousnesses as their primary and secondary components.
Therefore, moment after moment, one cannot be separated from this storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna); this is what is meant by abiding in cessation.
Although one may attain meditative concentration, as for the mind abiding within defilement and purity, how could the faculties be made empty? How could consciousness be eliminated?
The awakening of the Hīnayāna does not reach this level; how then could it fully realize nirvāṇa?
The vast and boundless Tripitaka cannot be exhausted.

Taking the sense of "grasping seeds" as the *ālaya* (storehouse), taking the sense of "receiving perfuming" as the "contained," and taking the sense of "maintaining seeds" as the "container. The verse says:
"All dharmas are stored within consciousness; consciousness and dharmas are likewise so. They are mutually the nature of cause and effect, and they are also always..."
The nature of causality; this is the inexhaustibility of the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Yet, the Buddha-dharma has no "many children" [it is not something easily multiplied];
it is difficult to encounter over vast eons. If a person can directly realize it, they are directly complete in it. For ten thousand ages, one gazes at the new moon in a clear blue pool;
yet upon turning the head, it is still within the old tower.
The abyss is deep and the seven waves are stirred by the wind of objects;
the waves and their source are mutually dependent. When struck by the wind of objects, many waves arise. The five, six, and seven consciousnesses all rely upon the eighth consciousness;
when deluded by the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*), then defiled and pure phenomena flow forth from it without end. Thus, while a single consciousness is deluded, [the manifold arises].
The seeds of consciousness and consciousness itself are both impure. How is this different from the seven waves being struck by the wind of objects?

One teaching states that the eight consciousnesses, whether manifest or as seeds, are like waves, while the four conditions such as objects are like the wind. If it is the wind of the four conditions—
Constantly striking the eighth consciousness manifests water; thus, the waves of the eighth consciousness’s manifest and seed states are perpetually stirred up.

Just as the seventh consciousness takes the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as its object, it acts as the wind that conditions the object, thereby agitating the waves of the eighth consciousness’s active manifestations.
If the active manifestations of the first seven consciousnesses permeate this storehouse consciousness, then this—
The manifest activities serve as the winds of the objective realm, which stir the seeds within the *ālayavijñāna*, giving rise to the waves of manifest activity.

Because these waves are inexhaustible, they are said to be "unfathomable. If one awakens to the nature of these eight consciousnesses, they become the Indra’s net jewels of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazangjie*).

The eighth consciousness—the root-body and the vessel-world—is the sovereign of total retribution; it is capable of maintaining the seeds of all phenomena, both out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*).

It maintains these seeds and is able to receive the perfuming of the preceding seven consciousnesses because it possesses four characteristics: first, the characteristic of firm abiding; second, the characteristic of being... [text truncated]

1. The nature of being recorded (the capacity for memory). 2. The nature of being perfumable. 3. The nature of being in conjunction with that which perfumes. 4. [The nature of] the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world.

Since these originally constitute the objective realm of the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect) transformed by the eight consciousnesses, when the mind takes the mind as its object, it is precisely these faculties and the world that serve as the perfumed and the supported.
If one views them with the pure eye, these faculties are nothing more than like spit.
Therefore it is said: "Seeing and hearing are like dreams and illusions; the three realms are like flowers in the sky.

When one departs from this life and arrives before the next as the presiding lord about to enter the womb, this eighth consciousness arrives first, and only then do the preceding seven consciousnesses follow in succession.
From birth onward, the causes of wholesome and unwholesome karma created by the preceding seven consciousnesses are all received as their retributive fruits within the eighth consciousness.

As the verse says: "The sages [receive it] in the crown of the head; those born in the heavens, in the eyes; humans, in the heart; evil spirits and ghosts, in the belly; and animals, in the kneecaps."
The "footplate of hell" symbolizes the departure after these eight consciousnesses have emerged; it is distinguished according to defilement and purity.
An ancient said: "As soon as one leaves the womb, one enters another. When the sages contemplate this, they feel profound sorrow;
this illusory body is ultimately devoid of fragrance or purity. "Shatter the painted vase and return home! How profound these words are!
Prior to the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), one merely abandons the "store" (*ālaya*);

this very *ālaya-vijñāna* is then purified through perfect awakening. Through these eight consciousnesses, one traverses the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), followed by the Joyful Stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the Luminous Wisdom Stage (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), the Difficult to Conquer Stage (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), and the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).

Having traversed the various stages (*bhūmi*) and awakened to the *tathatā*-mind, it is called the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). At this point, all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted and all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are shattered.
Both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), as well as images with external referents (*sanimitta*) and those without (*nirnimitta*), are simultaneously empty.

Thus, the internal grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) no longer functions, and one realizes the ninth consciousness, the Pure White Consciousness (*vimala-vijñāna*), while the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is just about to be relinquished. Nevertheless, one must still maintain adherence to these hierarchical stages.

"Is this not precisely what breaks open the treasury? Master Xuanzang said: "The first five consciousnesses are called 'perfectly luminous' (*yuanming*); their initial arising constitutes the attainment of the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
The sixth is called 'the arousal of the initial mind on the Stage of Joy' (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). The seventh is called 'the nature of equality of the extremely joyful initial mind.

The eighth is called 'the great, perfectly round, and stainless simultaneous arousal. These terms—'initial mind' and 'simultaneous'—refer to a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) of a Mahāyāna practitioner."
This is the stage of awakening that transcends the level of equal enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). How could it truly be the result of so much refinement?
After the Vajra Path, there is the emptiness of maturation (*vipāka-śūnyatā*).
Regarding "ripening" (*vipāka*): it is so called because it is the fruit induced by wholesome or unwholesome [karma];

or because it ripens through transformation, or ripens at a different time, or ripens as a different category—thus it is termed "the nature of ripening. For example, while originally we were all together as Buddhas, yet I am currently not the same as the Buddha;
this is the full maturation of *karmic consciousness*. When karma reaches its point of maturation, one willingly becomes a sentient being, rather than unwillingly becoming one.
The Buddha said: "It is because of this single segment of greed and delusion within the eight seeds that even a thousand Buddhas find it difficult to save one.

Only by personally accepting responsibility and being able to believe in the matter of one's own fundamental nature can one do so. If one uses pure vajra-wisdom to break through the self and break through phenomena, then afflictions will be eliminated once and for all;
even the effort of drilling wood for fire will be forgotten, and those who cling to pure dharmas will likewise be emptied along with them."
The Great Perfect Circle, stainless and arising simultaneously, universally illuminates the lands within the atoms of the ten directions.

When the ālayavijñāna (the storehouse consciousness), the empty state, and the vipāka (maturation) are relinquished, then the five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness become pure awakening in a single kṣaṇa, without awaiting a second moment.
This is because the manifesting consciousness, the evolving consciousness, and the storehouse consciousness are three in one, and one in three.

Because they are one, they function as a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). Thus, at the mere thought of them, they appear vividly, like a treasury of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-kośa*) that is entirely free from obstruction.
Therefore, sometimes the manifest [consciousness] gives rise to the latent storehouse; sometimes the storehouse gives rise to the evolving consciousness;

and sometimes the evolving consciousness gives rise to both the manifest and the storehouse. This is because each consciousness and its objects possess their own respective seeds, yet are able to manifest simultaneously.

These consciousnesses and their objects each share a single seed, yet they are able to manifest one another. For this reason, I say that while their substance is identical, their functions are distinct; this is precisely the meaning [of the teaching].
However, the sense-faculties belong to the objective aspect (nimittabhāga), while consciousness belongs to the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga).

From the subjective aspect, the objective aspect arises; from the objective aspect, the subjective aspect arises. Without the root [of a separate self], the subjective and objective aspects are identical to false conceptualization (vikalpa). False conceptualization...
Fundamentally empty, it is originally pure awakening. Thus, luminosity is not separate from darkness, and consciousness is not separate from its nature.
Throughout all time, past and present, every person is fully endowed with the stainless mirror. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Verses on Consciousness-Only) says:

"To posit even a slight object before oneself and claim it is the nature of consciousness-only—because there is something apprehended, one does not truly abide in consciousness-only. This is a refutation of those who do not penetrate the ultimate teaching.

Alas! Because the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) is not clearly understood, people conversely take this school of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇayāna) to be the establishment of self-nature, thereby creating obstacles for themselves. Is this not truly a cause for deep lamentation?
According to the Treatise on Consciousness, not a single thing can be established before one's eyes; yet those who claim to be men of great knowledge still speak of "mind" and "nature."

How can one be so full of venom as to spew it upon others? You should know that every consciousness possesses a gate of awakening. With a secret golden needle, I shall guide you to join with the bamboo shoot.

As for what is called the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), the five object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*), the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala*), and the twenty-six afflictions (*kleśa*)—if you look at them with an open eye, what exactly are they in the end? Do not mistake them for mere shadows of dharmas.
One then takes it as one's own food and drink. It is as if there were something within the breast that one ultimately cannot let go of.
One must also open one's eyes and observe its form: where exactly does it reside?
When one has scrutinized and seen through it all, it is truly not worth even a single laugh from me. Therefore, I say: "Ten billion dust motes..."
To exhaust oneself to the point of endangering even the subtle life-faculty—how is this different from blowing air into a net or hiding a sound inside a box?

Thus, the ignorant cling to the two types of awakening—the equal and the sublime—and employ the methods for purifying death to restrain practitioners. Even if they achieve some realization, is it not still a case of binding their hands and feet?
Although they claim the mind is empty while objects are not, and that they destroy attachment but not phenomena, in the end, this remains [merely] *amṛta* (nectar).
This nectar-like poison is simply the wielding of the vajra sword to strike the head, cutting off that head atop the crowns of the thousand Buddhas;
this is how one expels the resentment of the Honored One Ānanda. Otherwise, to produce much tangled verbiage would surely result in being spat upon by the Great Master Xuanzang.
